articles.title: Araceli Lemos defende cancelamento da concessão de água no Pará | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidatos do Podemos e do MDB faltaram ao encontro promovido pela TV Norte SBT Pará. Postulante do PSOL criticou ausências e prometeu extinguir contrato de concessão do saneamento básico no estado.
articles.summary: Candidatos do Podemos e do MDB faltaram ao encontro promovido pela TV Norte SBT Pará. Postulante do PSOL criticou ausências e prometeu extinguir contrato de concessão do saneamento
articles.body:
Araceli Lemos, do PSOL, concede entrevista à TV Norte SBT Pará, após Dr Daniel e Hana Ghassan se ausentarem em debate. — Foto: Reprodução / TV Norte SBT Pará

A candidata ao governo do Pará pelo PSOL , Araceli Lemos , afirmou que vai cancelar o contrato de privatização da água e do esgoto, se eleita no Pará. As declarações foram feitas em entrevista à TV Norte SBT Pará nesta sexta-feira (18).

"Uma das primeiras medidas será rever esse contrato de privatização. Colocar abaixo esse contrato, porque contrato em que tem duas partes que assinam e uma não cumpre com a sua responsabilidade, é passível sim de ser revisto", afirmou Araceli.

Araceli compareceu à sede da TV Norte SBT Pará, em Belém, para participar de um debate com outros postulantes à chefia do Executivo estadual. No entanto, os demais convidados — a atual governadora Hana Ghassan (MDB) e o ex-prefeito de Ananindeua, Dr Daniel (Podemos) — não compareceram.

Segundo a emissora, o candidato Dr Daniel não havia confirmado participação. Hana Ghassan, de acordo com a emissora, confirmou presença e, uma hora antes do início do debate, a assessoria enviou um e-mail cancelando a participação sob a justificativa de "incompatibilidade de agenda".

As outras três candidatas na disputa são Gal Leite (UP), Ruth Reis (Democrata) e Well Macêdo (PSTU) ficaram de foram porque seus partidos, federações ou coligações não possuem o mínimo de cinco representantes no Congresso Nacional — critério utilizado na realização do debate.

A entrevista de Araceli teve cerca de 26 minutos e formato adaptado devido à ausência dos concorrentes. Ao longo do momento, ela respondeu perguntas do jornalista Ranier Bragon, do SBT News de Brasília, sobre saneamento, segurança, corrupção e alianças políticas. Veja como foi:

🎙️ Saneamento básico e concessão de água

A candidata do PSOL criticou a ausência dos concorrentes e falou de propostas. No saneamento, ela classificou a situação do setor no estado como "a maior crise de água já existente no Pará", apontando problemas como mau cheiro, gosto ruim na água que chega às torneiras e cobranças indevidas, inclusive sobre poços artesianos cavados pela própria população.

"Nós vamos rever, nós vamos colocar abaixo esse contrato e vamos investir numa companhia que leve água para todas as famílias", disse Araceli.

Ao ser questionada sobre a impopularidade da gestão do ex-prefeito de Belém, Edmilson Rodrigues (PSOL), Araceli argumentou que a capital padece de uma limitação orçamentária severa e que necessita de parcerias com as esferas estadual e federal.

Segundo ela, a prefeitura de Belém sofreu um "boicote" e um "movimento de puxação de tapete" por parte do governo do estado.

Como proposta para combater desvios, a candidata prometeu implementar mecanismos de transparência ativa, fiscalização rigorosa de obras públicas e a criação de canais de participação popular regionalizada para que a própria população decida as prioridades orçamentárias e fiscalize a aplicação dos recursos.

A candidata alertou para o crescimento de 24% nos casos de feminicídio no Pará e criticou a atual estrutura de proteção às mulheres.

Segundo ela, dos 144 municípios do estado, apenas cerca de 25 contam com Delegacias da Mulher (DEAMs), e somente quatro funcionam 24 horas.

"O meu governo vai ter delegacia em todos os municípios. No meu governo vai ter delegacia funcionando 24 horas. No meu governo vai ter política de prevenção, porque mais do que combater, do que chegar na consequência, é evitar que a mulher seja assassinada", propôs Araceli.

Ela também defendeu a criação de linhas de crédito para a autonomia financeira de mulheres vítimas de violência e a construção de casas-abrigo estaduais.

🎙️ Alianças nacionais e apoio a presidenciáveis

Araceli comentou sobre, segundo ela, o crescimento da extrema-direita no Pará, atribuindo parte dessa ascensão à falta de posicionamento firme do atual governo estadual e da candidata Hana Ghassan, atual governadora, em relação a apoio para a Presidência da República.

Ela também criticou o Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT) por ter se coligado à família Barbalho no estado, classificando a decisão como um "equívoco histórico".

A candidata destacou que o PSOL apoia formalmente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, candidato à reeleição na Presidência da República pelo PT, e foi o primeiro partido a inaugurar a "Casa Lula" no Pará, realizando a campanha do presidente desde a pré-campanha.

Nas considerações finais, Araceli Lemos destacou a trajetória como professora e filha de um operário da Cosanpa, além de prometer um salário mínimo regional de R$ 2.200; e zerar o tempo de espera por exames e consultas especializadas.

O primeiro turno das eleições está marcado para o dia 6 de outubro. Em caso de segundo turno, a votação será realizada no dia 27 de outubro.

articles.title: Eleições 2026: veja como foi o dia dos candidatos ao Governo do Maranhão nesta sexta (18) | G1
articles.standfirst: Veja como foram as atividades de campanha de André Luís, Dimas Cassimiro, Eduardo Braide, Felipe Camarão, Orleans Brandão, Reginaldo Lima, Roberto Rocha e Saulo Arcangeli.
articles.summary: Veja como foram as atividades de campanha de André Luís, Dimas Cassimiro, Eduardo Braide, Felipe Camarão, Orleans Brandão, Reginaldo Lima, Roberto Rocha e Saulo Arcangeli.
articles.body:
Candidatos ao Governo do Maranhão cumpriram compromissos de campanha nesta sexta-feira (18). As agendas incluíram visitas a municípios, entrevistas, caminhadas, reuniões e atividades relacionadas a propostas para mobilidade e transporte público.

O primeiro turno das eleições será realizado no dia 4 de outubro. Já o segundo turno, caso necessário, está marcado para 25 de outubro.

O candidato André Luis realizou uma panfletagem no período da tarde nas proximidades do Terminal da Praia Grande, em São Luís , com foco em propostas para o transporte público no Maranhão.

Durante a agenda, ele afirmou que pretende reorganizar o setor e dividir as empresas de transporte em três áreas: garagem, veículos e rodoviários.

Segundo o candidato, entre as propostas estão a realização de uma nova licitação para empresas de ônibus e medidas voltadas para a renovação da frota e melhorias salariais para trabalhadores do setor.

O candidato Orleans Brandão cumpriu agenda nas regiões do Alto Turiaçu e Vale do Pindaré. No fim da manhã, ele esteve em Governador Newton Belo, onde participou de um evento com eleitores e lideranças políticas. Em seguida, realizou uma caminhada no município.

Depois, Orleans seguiu para Bom Jardim. Durante as visitas, falou sobre propostas relacionadas à infraestrutura, transporte e mobilidade urbana.

O candidato afirmou que pretende realizar obras de mobilidade em São Luís, incluindo a conclusão da Avenida Metropolitana e a expansão da Via Expressa.

Eduardo Braide foi entrevistado ao vivo no JM1, da TV Mirante, durante a manhã. À tarde, participou de uma caminhada em Dom Pedro. À noite, a agenda prevista inclui uma caminhada em Presidente Dutra.

Roberto Rocha participou, durante a tarde, de uma agenda com lideranças religiosas em São Luís. À noite, o candidato tem viagem prevista para Santa Inês.

Saulo Arcangeli gravou conteúdos para as redes sociais e participou de dois podcasts durante a manhã. À tarde, participou de outro podcast. À noite, está prevista a participação do candidato na inauguração da nova sede do PSTU, no bairro São Francisco, em São Luís.

Felipe Camarão participou, pela manhã, de uma reunião com lideranças quilombolas e gravou conteúdo para o programa eleitoral.

No período da tarde, participou de uma plenária com povos de terreiros e povos tradicionais e realizou uma caminhada no bairro Anjo da Guarda, em São Luís.

Até a última atualização desta reportagem, o candidato não havia divulgado compromissos de campanha.

A agenda divulgada anteriormente pelo candidato foi cancelada.

A disputa pelo governo do Maranhão em 2026 tem oito nomes anunciados como candidatos — Foto: Montagem g1

articles.title: Early voting begins in US midterm elections that could flip control of Congress
articles.summary: In-person voting for this year’s midterm elections began Friday, ushering in the final six weeks for Americans to decide which party they trust to lead Congr...
articles.body:
HENRICO, Va. (AP) — In-person voting for this year's midterm elections began Friday, ushering in the final six weeks for Americans to decide which party they trust to lead Congress through a cost-of-living crisis , a prolonged war in Iran and other pressing issues.

Election administrators say they are prepared and confident the vote will be accurate and secure. Nevertheless, President Donald Trump has continued efforts to denigrate certain voting methods and reshape how elections are run, through court challenges , a federal hunt for noncitizen voters and a pressure campaign to force election officials to share sensitive voter data.

Friday was the start of early voting in Virginia. Voters in a few other states, including Minnesota and South Dakota, can cast absentee ballots in person, typically at a local election office or voting center. More expansive early voting is scheduled to begin in those and other states in the coming weeks.

At a voting location in Fairfax, Virginia, 18-year-old college student Sanya Singhal was among the first to vote early in person Friday morning, arriving well before the site opened to get in line.

"Why not just have a little fun in life, you know, try to be the first early voter?" she asked. "I really want to participate in my democracy."

At a voting location in suburban Richmond, a poll worker rang a bell as the building opened and about a dozen voters in line began to file in. Stephen Gura was excited to be the first.

"This election is critical. We need to stop the Trump agenda," said Gura, who added that he voted for U.S. Sen. Mark Warner, a Democrat, and Shannon Taylor, the Democratic nominee against Republican incumbent Rob Wittman in the 1st Congressional District.

The Nov. 3 election includes votes for governor and state legislature in most states and will determine whether Republicans maintain control of the U.S. House and Senate. If Democrats retake Congress, it will alter the trajectory of the final two years of Trump's term, most likely leading to investigations and other oversight efforts.

Votes underway after redistricting and Trump's bid to control how elections are run

At the suburban Richmond voting center, a steady stream of voters flowed in and out. William Curry, a 74-year-old retiree who described himself as a libertarian-leaning independent conservative, voted for Warner's Republican challenger, Bert Mizusawa, and Wittman. Curry said he generally approves of the job Trump has done, apart from the war with Iran.

"He's in a mess he can't get rid of," Curry said of the conflict.

On a rainy day in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, Bill Goehring, 67, said he voted early at the county office because he will be traveling later. He voted for a mix of Democrats and independents, and said Trump's "dictatorial tendencies are bad for America."

John Thomas, a conservative retired police officer at the Sioux Falls office, said his biggest concerns were public safety and election integrity. He said he doesn't want to see votes in federal elections from immigrants living in the country illegally. Such fraudulent voting has been found to be extremely rare.

Trump's immigration agenda is "spot on," the 77-year-old said.

"We wouldn't be a country that much longer if it had stayed the same for another four years," he said.

The start of early voting comes at a time of deep angst and division among many Americans about issues including rising gas and grocery prices , the war in Iran, the looming risks of artificial intelligence and Trump's aggressive immigration enforcement campaign .

It also follows an unprecedented spate of mid-decade redistricting for the House that began when Trump urged the Republican-controlled legislature in Texas to redraw its congressional map to help the party. California and other states followed.

The changes affect millions of people: Research shows 1 in 10 Americans this fall is a resident of a different congressional district than in 2024.

Those partisan efforts are expected to continue before the 2028 elections after a landmark ruling this year from the U.S. Supreme Court weakened the federal Voting Rights Act's protections against racially discriminatory redistricting .

As the start of early voting approached, Trump was focused on efforts to assert federal control over election administration, even as the Constitution bestows the power to run elections on the states and, in some cases, Congress. The nation's highest court this week rejected Trump's bid to restrict mail ballots, but several of his administration's other efforts to influence the voting process and investigate state voter lists continue.

Virginia's Democratic attorney general warned Thursday that Trump's administration may have violated the state's laws after a whistleblower accused federal employees of misrepresenting themselves on voter lookup tools to hunt for noncitizen voters .

Trump for years has raised the specter of widespread noncitizen voting in U.S. elections, and this year is no exception. But research continues to show noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare .

David Becker, executive director and founder of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said he wouldn't be surprised if the Republican president continues "his disinformation campaign and his attack on election officials." But he said he thinks "the process will hold as it has in past years."

At least a few Friday voters were motivated to vote early in part because of Trump's actions.

In Minneapolis, 47-year-old business processing engineer Dragan Colakovic said he didn't want to wait until Election Day for fear of being stopped by immigration agents. He said Trump's surge of agents to Minnesota in an immigration crackdown earlier this year terrified him. He is a naturalized U.S. citizen who moved from Bosnia in 1997 and saw the horrors of war in the former Yugoslavia.

"This echoed what I saw in Bosnia," he said of the heavily armed immigration agents who repeatedly swept through his neighborhood, which has many immigrants.

"These were my neighbors, my friends," being arrested, he said.

Sixty-three-year-old Democratic voter Laura Bland in Virginia's Henrico County said she cast a ballot early to send "a signal that we're still here" despite Trump's efforts to curtail mail voting.

"Regardless of whether you vote for a Democrat, Republican, people are not going to be stopped or intimidated from participating in our elections," Bland said, nearly moved to tears.

Advocates suggest voters cast their ballots early

Voting rights advocates have encouraged voters this year to cast mail ballots early, in part because of concerns about recent changes in U.S. Postal Service operations that could delay the application of postmarks to ballots.

Voting early "gives voters options, eases lines on Election Day and can even mean faster results," said Hannah Fried, co-founder and CEO of the voting rights group All Voting Is Local.

The top official at the U.S. Postal Service also encouraged voters who cast ballots by mail to get them in a week before they're due.

"Everything is solved if people vote early," Postmaster General David Steiner said in an interview .

In a news briefing Thursday, Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon urged people not to be swayed by stories they might have seen or read that cast doubt on election operations. They would be able to vote "just like they always have," he said.

"I just want to reaffirm that Minnesota's elections are fundamentally free, fair, accurate, honest and secure," he said.

Swenson reported from New York and Raza from Sioux Falls, S.D. Associated Press writers Mike Catalini in Philadelphia, Tim Sullivan in Minneapolis, and AP video journalist Nathan Ellgren in Fairfax, Va., contributed to this report.
authors: ALI SWENSON, SARAH RANKIN and SARAH RAZA

articles.title: Election 2026: Earls roars ahead of Stevens by nearly 11% in new poll
articles.summary: (The Center Square) – Incumbent Democratic Justice Anita Earls has roared ahead of Republican challenger Sarah Stevens in polling for North Carolina’s lone s...
articles.body:
Incumbent Democratic Justice Anita Earls is leading Republican challenger Sarah Stevens in polling for North Carolina’s state Supreme Court election, with Earls ahead by 47.2%-36.4% in the latest sampling.

In the nationally watched election to succeed Republican Sen. Thom Tillis in the U.S. Senate, Democrat Roy Cooper is leading Republican Michael Whatley by 49.2%-34.1%, showing an increase in Cooper's lead since August.

Absentee voting in North Carolina began on Sept. 4, with the mailing of ballots to nearly 50,000 requesting them, and the voter registration deadline is Oct. 9, with early in-person voting scheduled for Oct. 15-31.

(The Center Square) – Incumbent Democratic Justice Anita Earls has roared ahead of Republican challenger Sarah Stevens in polling for North Carolina's lone state Supreme Court election.

Earls leads 47.2%-36.4% in the Carolina Journal sampling conducted with Harper Polling. Respondents numbered 608 on Sunday through Tuesday earlier this week, and the analysis carries a +/- 3.97% margin of error.

The August polling by Carolina Journal on the race had Earls up 43.3%-39.7% though within the +/- 4% margin of error for a statistical tie; Earls led in May 41.3%-35.6% outside the +/- 4% margin of error; and Earls led in March 40.6%-38%, also a statistical tie within the +/- 4% margin of error.

In August, Earls led Stevens 47%-44% in a High Point University Poll that was a statistical tie having landed within the +/- 4.3% margin of error. In a July sampling by Public Policy Polling, the duo was also statistically tied inside a +/- 3.6% margin of error with Earls up 44%-42%.

Earls, a Seattle native, was a founder of the Southern Coalition for Social Justice before winning election to the Supreme Court in 2018. Stevens resigned from the North Carolina House of Representatives effective June 16 to focus on her campaign, having served District 90's Surry and Wilkes counties in the northwestern region of the state along the Virginia border.

For the nationally watched election to succeed Republican Sen. Thom Tillis in the U.S. Senate, Democrat Roy Cooper leads Republican Michael Whatley 49.2%-34.1%. That's an increase on August when Cooper led 51.5%-39%, in May when Cooper led 49.8%-38.7%, and in March when Cooper led 48.9%-41.1%.

Asked "how likely would Roy Cooper be to support the policy priorities of the Democratic Socialists of America if elected," respondents overwhelmingly connected him at 60.1%-20.7% for likely or not likely.

The Democratic Party, on a national scale, has tension in an ideological tussle for control. Democratic socialism is on the rise, replete with a desire not only for social reforms but also restructuring, including abolishing the U.S. Senate, having Congress pick the president and U.S. Supreme Court, defunding the Pentagon, and allowing all residents, regardless of citizenship, to vote.

The poll was 73.9%-9.2% on likely to not likely.

Absentee voting began on Sept. 4 with the mailing of ballots to the nearly 50,000 requesting them, opening a 61-day window to Nov. 3. Oct. 9 is the voter registration deadline.

Absentee requests do not require a reason; anyone can file with their respective counties. The deadline for an absentee ballot in the mail to be in a county election board office is when the polls close at 7:30 p.m. on Nov. 3; the request deadline is 5 p.m. on Oct. 20.

Early in-person voting is Oct. 15-31, and same-day registration is permitted.

North Carolinians will choose a U.S. senator, all 14 members of the U.S. House, and all 170 members of the General Assembly. One state Supreme Court seat and a number of judges, district attorneys, and county level offices are on the state's second-longest ballot of the four-year cycles.

Cooper's bid to succeed Tillis would be trend-breaking if successful. Tillis, Richard Burr and Ted Budd have made Republicans 5-for-5 since Democrat Kay Hagan won election to the U.S. Senate in 2008.

Republicans in statewide races for this decade – 2020, 2022 and 2024 – are 32-10 against Democrats, a party with significantly declining voter registrations for more than 20 consecutive years.

This U.S. Senate seat is viewed as a major player nationally in the quest for a majority in the chamber. Republicans have 53 seats today. In no particular order, Ohio, Michigan, Georgia, Maine, Iowa, New Hampshire, Alaska, Texas and Montana are the other top battlegrounds among 35 races. Two of those are special elections, the other 33 are in regular rotation.

articles.title: D.C. Official to Trump Admin: Scrap Arch, Build 1925 Columns
articles.summary: D.C. Official to Trump Admin: Scrap Arch, Build 1925 Columns
articles.body:
A District of Columbia preservation official urged the Trump administration to scrap the planned 250-foot triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery and instead build the two slender columns envisioned in a 1925 congressional plan.

The arch would "effectively replace much of the important view with a frame" between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington, according to the D.C. Historic Preservation Office.

The Committee of 100 on the Federal City and residents from every state and most U.S. territories have expressed opposition to the arch, with 93% of D.C. resident comments opposing the project.

Andrew Lewis, an official in D.C.'s Historic Preservation Office, made the case for the columns in a Wednesday letter first reported by The Washington Post. The arch would "effectively replace much of the important view with a frame" between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington, Lewis said.

Trump has cited the 1925 congressional plan , which authorized two 166-foot columns symbolizing post-Reconstruction reunification of North and South, as his legal authority for the 250-foot arch.

Lewis countered that the arch would break the historic sightline between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House, the former home of Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee, which the columns were designed to preserve.

The Committee of 100 on the Federal City, a nonprofit preservation group, made a parallel argument in its own letter Wednesday, accusing the National Park Service of failing to weigh alternative sites and designs.

An Interior Department spokesperson defended the process, telling The Washington Sun the agency has followed all laws and logged more than 100,000 public comments .

"To infer this process is unlawful shows a lack of understanding of the facts," the spokesperson said.

A D.C. review cited in the letter found opposition from residents of every state and most U.S. territories, with 93% of the roughly 11,000 D.C. resident comments opposing the arch.

The Trump-appointed U.S. Commission of Fine Arts granted final approval in May, and the National Capital Planning Commission voted for preliminary approval in July.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced excavation work this month, though the administration said it was for information gathering, not construction, with the planning commission's final vote still pending.

articles.title: Trump breaks with many Republican midterm candidates, voters on key tech issues
articles.summary: Polling shows voter skepticism of AI, data centers and Flock cameras.
articles.body:
In the final months before the high-stakes midterm election, President Donald Trump has come out against regulation on controversial tech issues from artificial intelligence to data centers to Flock cameras -- positions that don't jibe with several Republican candidates' running in this midterm election.

Trump has dismissed concerns from lawmakers and AI developers about potential dangers of AI development, calling it a "hoax" and arguing against comprehensive federal regulation. Trump said in social media posts that regulation would put American AI development at a disadvantage to China.

In Michigan, GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers has called for a "national security framework" on AI and to "slow down development of AI in order to allow the government and its partners to catch up."

His opponent Dr. Abdul El-Sayed used the president's statements on AI regulation as an attack against Rogers.

"Donald Trump always puts his own interests over the interests of the rest of us. And Mike Rogers, he's going to put whatever Donald Trump wants over you, and that's the danger," El-Sayed said in a forum this week with a local news station.

Rogers has not publicly responded to El-Sayed's comments.

In Texas, Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, the state's attorney general, has pitched himself as a champion of big tech regulation. On the campaign trail, Paxton has touted his lawsuits against major social media companies and his calls for restrictions on the ability of AI bots to interact with underage users.

Paxton hasn't weighed in on potential safety risks coming out of major AI companies. His campaign did not respond to specific questions about his stances on federal regulation on AI.

Paxton's Democratic opponent, state Sen. James Talarico, unveiled an AI regulatory platform in his campaign launch -- focused largely on advocating against job losses due to AI and on greater export controls on AI chips.

In an appearance alongside businessman Mark Cuban last month, Talarico talked about the need for comprehensive federal guardrails on AI.

Polling shows that Americans are concerned about the role that AI is playing in our lives, a Marquette poll conducted earlier this month found about two-thirds of adults saying AI is a bad thing for society.

A March Quinnipiac University poll found 74% of Americans saying that the government was not doing enough to regulate AI; just 13% said the government was doing enough.

Data centers are another key issue ahead of the midterm elections where Trump -- who has defended data center construction as an economic and national security win -- has differed with Republican candidates.

Rogers has called for a one year moratorium on new construction in Michigan. Republican Sen. Jon Husted, running for reelection in Ohio, is sponsoring legislation aimed at making data centers pay for their utility usage.

The president's own comments could pose difficulty for vulnerable Republican candidates as he continues with incendiary rhetoric, writing in a social media post last month that communities that oppose data centers "want to be backwards and poor."

Voter sentiment has shifted on the issue of data centers. The Marquette poll found 71% of adults said the costs of building data centers outweigh the benefits, up from 62% in January.

Controversial automatic license plate readers -- and their most common camera type, Flock -- have become an emerging political flashpoint in midterm races .

Trump said last month that he "sort of" likes them "because of law enforcement," acknowledging that some people "think it's an infringement." Advocates of the camera have argued that the cameras reduce crime and improve public safety.

In Wisconsin, Republican candidate for governor, Tom Tiffany, has called on a moratorium on state funding for flock cameras pending a new task force. His democratic opponent, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, has issued an order limiting the use of the cameras by the county.

In Pennsylvania, both Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and Republican challenger Stacy Garrity have publicly supported a ban on the cameras.

Highly publicized cases of misuse have swayed public sentiment on the use of the cameras by law enforcement.

The Marquette poll found 61% of Americans said the cameras are unacceptable violations of privacy rights while 39% said they are an important tool for police investigations.

Flock said in a statement to ABC News last month that the company has made changes aimed at ensuring privacy and welcome regulatory efforts.

"We support thoughtful, bipartisan legislation that puts strong privacy, transparency, and accountability guardrails in place while preserving law enforcement's ability to use technology responsibly to keep people safe," Flock said in the statement.

articles.title: Em ato, Marina Silva se confunde e troca próprio número pelo de Salles; vídeo | G1
articles.standfirst: Durante discurso em ato de campanha de Lula, candidata ao Senado por São Paulo citou o número 300, usado pelo adversário, mas se corrigiu na sequência.
articles.summary: Durante discurso em ato de campanha de Lula, candidata ao Senado por São Paulo citou o número 300, usado pelo adversário, mas se corrigiu na sequência.
articles.body:
A candidata ao Senado por São Paulo Marina Silva ( Rede ) se confundiu ao apresentar os números de urna de candidatos aliados durante um ato de campanha do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), na sexta-feira (18), em Guarulhos, na região metropolitana de São Paulo.

Ao pedir votos para os candidatos que participam da campanha, Marina citou o número 300 antes de corrigir a própria fala para 180. O número citado por ela é usado por Ricardo Salles ( Novo ), que também disputa uma das duas vagas ao Senado pelo estado.

“São Paulo vai eleger Haddad governador, Lula presidente, Simone 400 e Marina 300… e 180. É 180”, disse Marina durante o discurso.

A troca dos números não foi a única confusão de Marina durante a fala. Antes, ela afirmou que ela e Simone Tebet ( PSB ) eram candidatas ao governo de São Paulo.

Simone, que também disputa uma vaga no Senado, corrigiu a colega durante o evento.

O ato em Guarulhos contou ainda com a presença de Lula, da primeira-dama Janja Lula da Silva, do vice-presidente Geraldo Alckmin (PSB) e do candidato ao governo paulista Fernando Haddad (PT), além de Simone Tebet.

A Quaest divulga, na próxima quarta-feira (23), uma nova pesquisa com as intenções de voto para o governo do Ceará e também para o Senado. O levantamento foi encomendado pela TV Verdes Mares .

O questionário disponível no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) inclui um cenário de 1º turno com oito candidatos ao governo . A pesquisa vai simular também um cenário de segundo turno.

Já para o Senado, o levantamento vai apresentar o cenário com oito candidatos .

Segundo os dados enviados pela Quaest ao TSE, serão entrevistadas 900 pessoas de 16 anos ou mais, residentes no estado do Ceará, entre os dias 19 e 22 de setembro.

A margem de erro é de três pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança é de 95%. A pesquisa foi registrada no TSE sob o número CE-08268/2026 .

articles.title: Can Trump ban CNN, news outlets he doesn’t like from the White House?
articles.summary: The ban is the latest attack by Trump on media outlets that he perceives as unfavourable to his administration.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has taken the unprecedented step of announcing that several media outlets are to be banned from the White House, “immediately”.

On Friday, he took to his social media platform, Truth Social, to announce the ban, citing “reporting FAKE NEWS!” as the reason, with other outlets to follow.

Asked by reporters later on Friday what he meant, Trump said: “Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, The New York Times is fake news, The Washington Post is fake news.”

Which news outlets have been banned and why?

The US President banned CNN, MS NOW (formerly MSNBC) and Politico from reporting from the White House.

On Truth Social, he accused the outlets of propagating “fake news”. He added that the outlets “constantly write or report fiction or lies” about the Trump administration, but did not give any examples.

However, a short news conference at the White House on the same day revealed that it was likely a partisan issue, telling reporters the outlets “purposely write negative news” and seek to “diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration. And honestly, we’ve done a fantastic job.”

CNN denounced the move, saying it stands behind its White House team and their “fair and accurate reporting”.

“We have a right under the US Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government,” a CNN spokesperson told Al Jazeera. “Should the ban, which President Trump threatened, go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally protected right.”

Politico said it would “continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones. We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them.”

The news outlet’s communications team also pushed back on a separate Trump claim that Politico had received government subsidies, calling it “false” and saying it had “been thoroughly debunked”.

MS NOW did not immediately comment on Trump’s announcement.

The National Press Club was among several groups that immediately criticised the ban as an attack on the free press.

“Banning news organisations from the White House based on the administration’s disapproval of their coverage is a clear attempt to control which voices are allowed to witness and report on the exercise of presidential power,” said the group’s president, Mark Schoeff Jr.

“Someone needs to explain to President Trump how the First Amendment works,” said Tim Richardson, journalism and disinformation director at PEN America.

Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, said: “These outrageous attacks only demonstrate how scared he is of an informed public.”

What rights do White House journalists have and what is their job?

White House journalists report on the US president and what he says and does; they question officials at briefings, report on policy, and rotate through the small “press pool” that follows the president into the Oval Office and onto Air Force One.

The First Amendment protects what they publish, so the government can’t censor them or legally penalise them for their reporting.

Once press passes are offered, courts have ruled they can’t be denied or revoked arbitrarily.

The White House must follow fair standards and give notice and a chance to respond.

On that basis, CNN won a court order in 2018 restoring Jim Acosta’s revoked pass.

The ban follows the president’s decision last year to bar Associated Press reporters from the Oval Office, Air Force One and other events in retaliation for the news outlet’s decision not to follow his lead in changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico, which lies partially in Mexican and other waters, to the Gulf of America.

Throughout his second term, Trump and his administration have attacked certain media outlets in court and through regulatory action.

Trump has also lashed out at individual reporters in person or over social media.

Since returning to office, Trump has pursued other legal action against a variety of different outlets, including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and the BBC.

His administration is also involved in a long-simmering confrontation with ABC over renewal of its broadcast licences.

Can outlets challenge this ban in court?

After the AP ban, the news agency filed a lawsuit, and that case is ongoing.

In the 1977 Sherrill v Knight case, a federal appeals court ruled that although the White House is not required to open its doors to the news media, once it establishes press facilities for credentialed journalists, it cannot deny access based on the content of a journalist’s coverage.

The court held that any denial must serve a compelling government interest and that the journalist must receive notice, the chance to respond and a final answer in writing.

It remains unclear at this stage what legal recourse CNN, MS NOW (formerly MSNBC) and Politico could pursue.

Reporting from Washington, DC, Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher said Trump’s ban will likely be challenged soon.

“The United States has the First Amendment [of its Constitution] that says the government cannot restrict access to this sort of thing,” he said.

“Other presidents have been angry at press coverage before. Lyndon B Johnson used to rail about it. Richard Nixon wondered whether or not he could ban certain people from the White House as well. At every point, they were told it’s not a good look.”

articles.title: Kirk family has powerful evidence — but Utah law could derail wrongful death case: experts
articles.summary: Utah's broad government immunity statute could block the Charlie Kirk wrongful death lawsuit against Utah Valley University over alleged security failures.
articles.body: A Utah government immunity law could upend the Kirk family’s efforts to bring a wrongful death lawsuit against Utah Valley University over alleged security failures surrounding Charlie Kirk’s assassination. Attorneys for Kirk’s family filed a notice of intent to sue on Sept. 9, one day before the anniversary of his death. The filing alleges a series of security failures by the university, including declining additional police officers, failing to adequately address concerns from Kirk's security team and not having an adequate security plan in place for his visit. But legal experts say the Kirks face an uphill legal battle because Utah law grants government entities — including their officers and employees — broad immunity from lawsuits arising from a lengthy list of circumstances, including the performance or failure to perform discretionary functions and claims involving assault, battery, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution and civil rights violations. "Unfortunately, Charlie Kirk's family is going to have a very difficult time prevailing in a wrongful death case in Utah," Tenielle Brown, a University of Utah law professor, told Fox News Digital. "And that's because Utah's government immunity statute is phrased in such a way that says even if the state and UVU were reckless, they retain immunity in cases that arise out of a battery, and that would include gunshot wounds." JUDGE IN ACCUSED ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON'S CASE EXPLAINS WHY DEATH PENALTY REMAINS ON TABLE IN WRITTEN ORDER Kirk, 31, co-founded Turning Point USA in 2012 and grew the conservative youth organization into a major force on high school and college campuses nationwide. He was shot and killed while speaking at Utah Valley University in Orem on Sept. 10, 2025. Neama Rahmani, president of West Coast Trial Lawyers, told Fox News Digital that wrongful death claims against the government are already difficult for plaintiffs to win because government entities generally enjoy broad immunity from lawsuits stemming from assaults or batteries committed by third parties. "I've handled lack of security cases, including lack of security cases against the government," Rahmani told Fox News Digital. "They are tough because you are trying to hold the police or city, county or state responsible for someone else's criminal actions." But Rahmani suggested the Kirk family's strongest evidence could be a message from UVU Police Chief Jeffrey Long acknowledging concerns about rooftop access to the Sorenson Center, a building located "pretty close" to where Kirk was scheduled to speak. The Sorenson Center sits directly west of the Losee Center, where prosecutors say Tyler Robinson fired the shot that killed Kirk. In response to the security concerns, Long messaged Kirk's team, "I got you covered." TYLER ROBINSON HEARING ENDS WITHOUT RULING AS EVIDENCE DISMANTLES CHARLIE KIRK CONSPIRACY CLAIMS "That means they're gonna argue that they assume the responsibility to make sure Charlie Kirk was safe, and they failed to do so," Rahmani said of the Kirk family. "In cases where you have the government taking on a duty, that tends to be better than simply arguing that the government has a duty to protect everyone because we know that murders happen all the time, and you can't sue the government just because someone is killed." But Brown said Utah law can shield government officials from lawsuits even when they fail to perform their job functions. "There have been a number of cases where the plaintiffs and the family of the victims have sued for either wrongful death or battery," Brown told Fox News Digital. "And in some cases, the government did behave recklessly, and they could show carelessness and recklessness and the plaintiffs were not able to prevail because it arose out of a battery. And that's unusual. Most states don't have that broad of a statute." Brown pointed to the case of Mika Scott, a 19-year-old Utah Valley University student who sued Utah County and the Utah County Sheriff's Office after Shawn Leonard, a prisoner with a violent criminal record who had escaped from a work-release program, raped her in 2010. "They were supposed to screen inmates to make sure that they weren't violent," Brown told Fox News Digital. "And then when they went out in the community on the job sites, they were supposed to make sure that they were policing the boundaries so that these inmates couldn't escape and in a really terrible situation." "And she could have shown carelessness and maybe even recklessness, but because of the government immunity statute and because this claim arose out of a battery, she was not able to prevail against the state," Brown continued. CHARLIE KIRK SUPPORTERS RETURN TO SITE OF ASSASSINATION 1 YEAR LATER: ‘WE ARE STILL STANDING’ The Utah Supreme Court addressed the statute's language in its 2005 decision in Wagner v. Utah, which held that civil battery does not require an intent to cause physical or psychological injury. "The court said, it may not be prudent for the state to continue to retain immunity here," Brown told Fox News Digital. " And they're kind of signaling to the legislature that the legislature should probably change the statute to allow for suits in cases like Charlie Kirk's." "But the state has not revised the statute and so it still says very clearly that you can't sue the state if the claim arises out of a battery," Brown continued. Brown said state workers who are not elected cannot be held accountable at the ballot box for failing to do their jobs. "The president of UVU, the campus police, those people are not elected, and so if you were to say sovereign immunity is all about letting people decide whether they're state actors or careless at the ballot box, then you vote them out of office," Brown said. "That doesn't work," Brown continued. "That argument doesn't for the UVU president because nobody can vote them of office, nobody is having any political check on the campus police." Astrid Tuminez, who served as the school's president at the time of Kirk's assassination, stepped down from her position in May 2026 after eight years. She and Long are named in the filing by Kirk's family. "We are aware of the notice of claim," a Utah Valley University spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "UVU addresses legal matters consistent with our established processes. Our focus remains on supporting our campus community." articles.title: Dem’s data center attack in critical Senate race hits snag when money trail surfaces: 'Jekyll-and-Hyde'
articles.summary: Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown accepted $20,000 from Google's PAC while running ads attacking a Google data center in Lancaster, Ohio.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is targeting Republican Sen. Jon Husted over Ohio's growing data center industry in a new campaign ad that features a facility owned by Google — whose corporate PAC and lobbyists have contributed thousands of dollars to Brown's campaigns. The Sept. 4 ad features an Ohioan blaming Husted for spearheading "the push to bring data centers to Ohio" and linking their expansion to "higher electric bills." The facility featured in the ad, which opened in Lancaster in 2023, is owned by Google. Campaign finance records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Google's corporate PAC contributed $20,000 to Brown over his political career. Brown also received thousands of dollars from individuals who lobby for Google, including two whose firms have worked on permitting, grid reliability and energy affordability issues. WATCH: GOP SENATOR UNLOADS ON 'CREATURE OF WASHINGTON' CHALLENGER IN CRITICAL SENATE SHOWDOWN "Apparently Google is terrible enough to put in a campaign attack ad, but perfectly acceptable when the political contributions are coming in," Mehek Cooke, a GOP strategist and attorney in Ohio, said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "That is the contradiction Brown needs to answer. If Google’s Lancaster investment is so bad for Ohio, why was Google political money acceptable to Sherrod Brown?" Among the contributors are Google lobbyist Lisa Kountoupes, who donated $3,500 in March, and Google lobbyist Michael D. Smith, who donated a total of $10,200 to Brown since 2017, according to Federal Election Commission records. The contributions were made to Friends of Sherrod Brown, Brown's principal campaign committee. Kountoupes’s firm, Kountoupes Denham Carr & Reid, was hired by Google in December to lobby on "issues related to permitting reform" tied to the company's data center needs, Politico previously reported. Smith's firm, Cornerstone Government Affairs, reported lobbying for Google on "issues related to permitting reform for grid reliability and energy affordability," according to federal lobbying filings. FEC records show Brown also received a combined $6,000 over the past decade from three additional Google lobbyists. In a statement to Fox News Digital, Lauren Chou, a spokeswoman for Brown's campaign, highlighted Brown's opposition to Ohio's data center expansion, saying Husted "led the charge," but did not address Brown's past campaign contributions. "Husted is a ‘chief reason’ Ohio has 226 data centers and is ‘the face of data centers’ in Ohio," Chou wrote. "Ohioans shouldn’t be forced to subsidize these costs and Ohioans – not Jon Husted and his billionaire friends – should get to decide if data centers are built in their community." Cooke accused Brown of acting like his "Google relationship in Washington does not count," calling it "Jekyll-and-Hyde politics." FOX NEWS POLL: ECONOMIC ANXIETY AND CANDIDATE CONCERNS DEFINE OHIO SENATE RACE "For nearly five decades, Brown has sold himself as the plaid-shirt, working-class populist," she said. "He lost in 2024, and now he is back running the same playbook: say one thing to Ohioans while his Washington record tells a very different story." Brown, who is seeking to return to the U.S. Senate in the high-stakes race against Husted, was elected to the U.S. Senate in 2006 before losing his reelection bid in 2024 to Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio. But this isn’t the first time Brown’s comeback campaign has faced questions over conflicting positions. FOX NEWS POLL: DEMOCRATIC UNITY, REPUBLICAN CROSSOVERS SHAPE OHIO SENATE RACE In 2015, Brown celebrated the construction of an Amazon data center in central Ohio, saying in a press release the new facility "is great news for New Albany and central Ohio." Despite his public praise, Brown has become an outspoken critic of Ohio's growing number of data centers, a defining issue in Ohio politics ahead of the midterms. President Donald Trump has pushed to expand the facilities, warning that communities that block them would "end up being backwards and poor." But Cooke said this about more than one local data center. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "America is in a global race for AI, computing capacity and energy infrastructure," she said. "China is not slowing down because American politicians discovered that attacking data centers makes a convenient campaign commercial." In a statement to Fox News Digital, Husted campaign spokesperson Amy Natoce said that Brown failed Ohio families during his 32 years in Washington and is "once again resorting to lies instead of facing his abysmal record head-on. " "The House overwhelmingly passed Sen. Husted’s bipartisan legislation requiring data center companies to pay for the power they use, but Senate Democrats blocked it," Natoce said. "Sherrod Brown and his friends would rather play politics and stick Ohio families with higher electric bills than pass a commonsense solution. It’s despicable."

articles.title: Iowa has become tricky territory for GOP in midterm election homestretch
articles.summary: Iowa Republicans are being presented with the difficult choice of embracing President Trump in the final stretch of the midterms as Democrats seek to tie them to the administration. The dynamic was on full display in Council Bluffs on Friday, when Iowa gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn joined Vice President Vance on the campaign trail, but…
articles.body:
Iowa Republicans are being presented with the difficult choice of embracing President Trump in the final stretch of the midterms as Democrats seek to tie them to the administration.

The dynamic was on full display in Council Bluffs on Friday, when Iowa gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn joined Vice President Vance on the campaign trail, but Republican Senate candidate Rep. Ashley Hinson opted to skip the event.

Hawkeye State Republicans are acutely aware of the risks of siding with the administration on issues like the Iran war.

Iowa Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R) and Zach Nunn (R) were among a group of seven House Republicans who voted with Democrats this week to block Trump from continuing the Iran war without approval from Congress.

All eyes were on the state’s Republican gubernatorial and Senate campaigns Friday with the vice president in town.

Hinson’s campaign cited scheduling conflicts ahead of the rally, but Vance still gave her a shoutout at the beginning of the event.

“I know she couldn’t be here today, but are we going to elect Ashley Hinson for United States Senator from the great state of Iowa?” Vance said, eliciting applause from the crowd.

Vance went on to tout Lahn’s candidacy before launching into a roughly seven-minute attack on Democratic gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand.

“The choice is this simple. It’s common sense versus crazy. It’s a man who listens to you versus a man who looks down on you. It’s a governor who fights for you versus a governor who fights against you,” Vance said.

“You have an opportunity to send not just Rob Sand but the entire Democrat Party a message: Check the crazy at the door, and learn to fight for Americans for a change,” he continued.

Polls show both races tightening, with Democrats holding a slight edge.

A poll released earlier this month from Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media shows Sand leading Lahn 49 percent to 46 percent. The same poll found Democratic Senate nominee Josh Turek leading Hinson 46 percent to 44 percent.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the Senate race as a “toss up” and the gubernatorial race as “lean Democratic.”

Hinson has shown other signs she is carefully navigating how to approach Trump and the administration in her race. Hinson attended last week’s GOP midterm convention in Dallas, but unlike other high-profile Republicans in attendance, she did not speak on stage.

“Zach Lahn and Ashley Hinson are two very different candidates, and they’re also facing two very different opponents,” said one Republican operative familiar with Iowa.

Lahn had strong support from the “Make American Healthy Again” (MAHA) movement in the Republican primary, scoring a major primary victory against Trump-backed candidate Rep. Randy Feenstra (R-Iowa).

Sand holds a fundraising and cash-on-hand advantage over Lahn. Many Republicans, including Vance, have hit Sand over receiving high-dollar contributions from family members.

Sand’s campaign fired back at Vance and Lahn in a statement, accusing the vice president of bailing the Republican nominee out.

“He’s bringing in another D.C. insider to try to bail him out because he can’t answer for his frequent flights to Kansas or his decade-long career as a political operative,” said Maddie Moher, Sand’s campaign press secretary.

“The attacks Lahn has pushed have been repeatedly found false by independent fact-checkers and news outlets, and outsourcing his talking points to another Washington politician doesn’t make them true. Iowa voters know the leader who will actually show up and work for them is Rob Sand,” she continued.

Miller-Meeks and Nunn were not in attendance at Friday’s rally, which did not take place in either of their congressional districts.

However, the pair made headlines along with five other Republicans for voting with Democrats on a war powers resolution earlier this week that would have curbed Trump’s power in continuing the war in Iran.

“It’s definitely notable,” said one national Republican operative, who added that other House Republicans facing uphill reelection bids voted with Democrats on the matter.

However, the operative pushed back on the notion that it is a sign vulnerable Republicans are running away from the administration.

Last month, Michigan Rep. Tom Barrett (R) voted in favor of a war powers resolution that would have limited Trump’s authority to continue the Iran war but appeared on stage with him at a rally in Michigan days later.

“I wouldn’t read into the war powers resolution as a way of ‘oh my god, our candidates are distancing themselves from Trump’ or anything. It’s more about this issue specifically,” the national Republican operative said, noting that Barrett, Miller-Meeks and Nunn are military veterans.

Nunn has also shown he is willing to appear with administration officials in his district, including Vance and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

“The reason you send Vance to Iowa or any administration official to any battleground is you want to fire up the base, and you want to turn out the base voters,” said the GOP operative familiar with Iowa.

articles.title: Trump ally Stephen Miller leads sweeping push to accelerate removal of migrant children
articles.summary: Exclusive: key White House loyalist orchestrating multi-agency effort condemned by critics as cruel and racist
articles.body:
Stephen Miller is leading an unprecedented and intense White House drive across a host of government departments to accelerate the removal of undocumented immigrant children from the US, using tactics that critics say are cruel and racist and, in some cases, flout federal law, the Guardian has learned.

As deputy chief of staff at the White House, focused on immigration policy, Miller is seen as the mastermind and enforcer behind Donald Trump's hardline anti-immigration agenda.

He is directing a whole-of-government approach that has been ramping up throughout Trump's second term and is targeting a vulnerable population of undocumented children. Many abruptly find themselves denied access to legal immigration pathways in the US, with their applications fast-tracked and then rejected before being forced out of the country.

Almost 200,000 children have been ordered removed from the US by immigration judges since Trump returned to the White House, a doubling of such court orders since January 2025, according to analysis of data from the Department of Justice's executive office for immigration review (EOIR) conducted by the California-based advocacy Mobile Pathways and shared with the Guardian. The advocacy group has focused its numbers on children appearing in immigration court, regardless of whether they arrived in the US alone or with family, and believes the total to be an undercount.

Miller has harnessed personnel and power for his task from at least five cabinet-level government departments, as described to the Guardian by several sources briefed on various initiatives, many of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation. The departments include Health and Human Services (HHS), which oversees the care of migrant children who are in the country without a parent or guardian; the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), where Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) are based; and the Department of Justice (DoJ), which houses the immigration courts – with the state department and the Department of Defense playing more subsidiary roles.

Miller frequently confers with subordinates, daily at times, pressing them to maximize removals of immigrant children from the US, according to a number of sources familiar with the White House plans.

"The folks that have to do the implementation are told, 'These instructions came directly from the White House,' or 'These instructions came directly from Stephen Miller,' as a way of conveying, you know, the importance of implementing them in a timely fashion and doing it in the way that they were instructed to do it," one source said.

Sources warned of the White House pushing each department to boost efforts individually and by working together in new ways to speed up and expand the deportation of undocumented children – especially by dismantling inter-agency communication safeguards designed to protect children, and hurrying them in vast numbers, without lawyers, in front of asylum officers and immigration judges who are either inclined or are under pressure to take a hard line and get them out of the US.

All departments involved, and the White House, were sent questions and asked for comment.

The White House did not deny that Miller is orchestrating a multi-agency effort to speed up the removal of undocumented children but claimed the effort was not new.

However, the White House and some other agencies that responded framed their endeavors as an anti-trafficking initiative instead of a means to enforcement.

"The Department of Homeland Security, the US Department of Health and Human Services, and the Homeland Security Council are working to locate and rescue these children. We are ensuring these children are reunited with their parents and families in their home countries," said White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis.

The Homeland Security Council is a body which, under Trump, now answers directly to him within the executive office of the president of the United States and is led by Miller.

But there is no certainty that deported young people end up reunited with family and safe in their home countries, as many of them left in the first place because of threats to their wellbeing, including from their own family, or in order to reunite with parents in the US.

One source said: "This administration has shown time and again that it has no plan for children other than to disrupt their lives and endanger them … they have no credibility to claim that they are acting with children's safety as their priority."

Claire Trickler-McNulty, an immigration policy fellow at Hyphen, a nonprofit intermediary focused on racial equity, said: "A facade of trafficking is sort of a convenient, feel-good cover that has nothing to do with trafficking and everything to do with reducing the program [of federal care for undocumented children], getting rid of services, getting rid of things they don't like, and then removing kids." Trickler-McNulty was previously an assistant director at ICE and a senior counselor at USCIS during the Biden administration.

Another source said of the Trump administration: "They are weaponizing that narrative [trafficking] because it makes them out to be the good guys, and everything else makes it really clear that they're not."

Critics point out that while there are some genuine instances of exploitation within the US that were exposed during the Biden administration, including by the New York Times , the Trump administration and other rightwing politicians and commentators are using extreme, and relatively rare, examples to justify their drastic intervention.

The sweeping inter-agency effort has also left more than 1,800 undocumented immigrant children stuck in the custody of federal health officials after often having previously experienced abuse, neglect, abandonment, trafficking or other harm in their countries of origin or on the way to the US. Sources believe many of those officials are collaborating with immigration enforcers while sharing children's confidential files in an unparalleled and legally dubious dismantling of bureaucratic safety firewalls.

One consequence of this strand of the anti-immigration crackdown is the sharp acceleration in the DoJ's immigration court orders to remove children from the US issued under the second Trump administration. This includes a rapid increase over this spring and summer. Removal orders rose from 7,366 a month in January 2025 to 16,200 in June, 16,750 in July and 14,744 in August, according to Mobile Pathways' research.

Of the more than 200,000 children in total that have been ordered removed under the second Trump administration, 70% were under the age of 13. The percentage of hearings ending in a removal order also more than doubled over the 20 months.

"What is my biggest fear? A lot of it is [already] happening," Trickler-McNulty said.

She is concerned by the administration gutting legal services and due process for children , closing down higher quality facilities, and having ICE officials take on senior roles in immigrant child welfare at HHS's office of refugee resettlement (ORR).

"Stephen Miller is incredibly involved in the whole immigration side, he has his daily calls, he reaches down into the agencies," she said.

Many unaccompanied children are facing the prospect of a forced return to dangerous situations in their countries of origin, particularly in Central America, including Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador, or even places as unstable as Afghanistan . Many have relatives in the US whom they could live with, who are vetted by the government and are known as sponsors. But the second Trump administration has severely restricted this from happening, either through new bureaucratic methods that keep children in custody until they can be deported, or by making prospective sponsors too scared of ICE to come forward.

Adults and families embroiled in the immigration system are subject to potential detention by DHS, while unaccompanied children are supposed to be quickly transferred from that department's agencies into the custody of ORR.

This divide is by congressional design, in recognition that children in the country alone should not rely for care on the same agency that is trying to deport them, experts said.

Yet as in other policy areas, this White House is prepared to break norms.

"The Trump administration has sacrificed every element of ORR's child welfare mission on the altar of higher deportation numbers," US senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, told the Guardian. "Instead of protecting kids from human trafficking or helping them reunite with family, Trump and officials at HHS and DHS are violating children's rights [and] flouting federal law to hit quotas and satisfy their ideological crusade against immigrants. The result is significant harm and trauma to innocent children."

ORR is responsible for providing the children with a safe place to live while ensuring they have access to legal information and thoroughly vetting their potential sponsors, usually family members, who apply for their release – serving a child welfare role that has historically been separate and apart from the nation's immigration enforcement arm.

Yet "there was a rollback of that really important firewall, and there was a lot more information sharing" that kicked off in Trump's second term, one source told the Guardian.

"It's clear from who leadership is and Miller's influence and the power dynamics of this administration that, you know, if DHS wants access to a child, they're going to get access to a child," another source said. "If ICE wants access to literally every single child's identifiable information, mental health records, behavioral records, all of that, they have it. I mean, it's not about sharing at this point. They just have access to it."

Half a dozen experts and government staff have detailed, as one put it, "an unprecedented level of collaboration between agencies like USCIS, ORR and ICE and the immigration courts".

Two sources described being briefed on the White House putting together a group of officials, known as "a tiger team" in government parlance, to coordinate policy around unaccompanied children, involving DHS, ORR, the DoJ and the state department.

The result is "coercive measure after coercive measure in trying to get kids to relinquish their rights". Experts interviewed for this article describe many measures and the extent to which they required inter-agency collaboration which have not been previously reported, including:

An influx of immigration and criminal enforcement officials joining ORR in key roles, with the likely effect of shifting the agency's priorities further away from child welfare and toward mass deportations, given the expertise and point of view of its new leadership and their known closeness with Miller.

ORR having ICE officers present – and sometimes waiting to detain people – at new in-person appointments that are now part of the sponsorship process, and the two agencies appearing to share information so that prospective sponsors are detained just before or shortly after a child is set to be released from federal custody, which critics believe is not a coincidence.

ORR seemingly collaborating with USCIS to schedule and rush through asylum adjudications for the children in their custody, sometimes through unorthodox, virtual interviews, not giving the children enough time to truly prepare or consult with attorneys.

ORR receiving feedback from the White House that its policy ideas were not sufficiently punitive and Miller forcing the agency to implement new tactics with the express purpose of increasing deportations among children and their family members.

Immigration judges allegedly being told by supervisors to rubber-stamp some of the requests by ICE's attorneys who are arguing to deport immigrants – including these children – in court, with the White House watching closely.

State department officials warning some countries of origin to expect increases in deported minors.

The Pentagon being asked by HHS to supply forensic auditors to scour for fraud among legal services organizations representing the children.

In a particularly dramatic case that a source suspects of involving inter-agency collusion, enforcement agents located and detained a small child's parent just one day before the child was going to be released from ORR custody and reunited with the parent.

Then, the source said, USCIS quickly asked the child's attorneys if they wanted to withdraw their client's asylum application – given that the child no longer had a relative available to care for them.

If it was, indeed, a tactic, it was successful: that family agreed to be deported so they could finally be together and free again.

Sources said that federal rules prohibit ORR from sharing children's welfare files with ICE and this wall had typically been effective but now was being routinely disregarded.

"They're taking norms that no-one ever thought needed to be legislated … because there was at least a general understanding of how harmful it would be if they were undone. And this administration just doesn't care about harm, right? The cruelty is the intent of this," a source said.

A state department spokesperson said: "The United States expects every country to accept the return of its nationals expeditiously. The state department leads diplomatic efforts to ensure compliance with this basic responsibility."

These practices are being implemented in tandem with other policies that are keeping children in foster homes, shelters or even secure lockups, away from family, for very long periods, where many lose hope and choose to self-deport. Hundreds of undocumented children are currently being sent to Texas , where it is easier to deport them.

Federal officials have also defunded over 20,000 unaccompanied children's attorneys from nearly a hundred legal services organizations across the country, while approaching firms and anti-trafficking organizations with little immigration law experience but with ties to the administration or ICE to replace them.

Meanwhile, in a message shared with the Guardian, a Department of Defense (DoD) personnel manager sent out a recruiting request saying that the health department was urgently looking for lawyers to represent the children, seemingly from within DoD itself, which manages the nation's military. The message encouraged recipients to pursue an encore career in government and continue serving their country, touting an expedited hiring process, a $10,000 signing bonus and a competitive benefits package.

The message is unusual because it indicated the involvement of the Pentagon in child welfare and immigration matters, and because of its apparent attempt to recruit military personnel who may have only the most rudimentary understanding of immigration law and little training in trauma-informed legal representation.

"HHS considered recruiting and detailing military lawyers for temporary augmentation of capacity but is no longer pursuing this option," an unnamed HHS spokesperson told the Guardian in a statement.

The Department of Defense referred questions to the White House and HHS.

"The erosion of due process , the dramatic attacks on both immigration courts and legal service providers , all of these feel like they are tools that are part of this larger project of essentially deporting these children by any means necessary," said Azadeh Erfani, director of policy at the National Immigrant Justice Center (NIJC).

For some experts, Miller's widely recognized leadership of the inter-agency effort is itself concerning because of his engagement with white nationalist ideology. Miller's rhetoric frequently echoes the "great replacement theory", a racist notion that nonwhite immigrants will overrun western civilization.

For his part, Trump has said that immigrants in the US from around the world are "poisoning the blood of our country" – a line that drew comparisons to Nazism.

"There is little doubt that Stephen Miller's influence on these anti-children policies comes with racial bias," said Erfani.

Another source added: "There's some real animus towards the kids coming from Miller and his acolytes. And I think that it's also very connected to the same reason that he wants to get rid of birthright citizenship. It's about demographics, right? And he sees the kids as, like, the future generation that will, you know, continue a multiracial, multicultural vision of this country."

Miller's departmental subordinates include a number of immigration enforcement veterans who have switched from ICE to immigrant child welfare in the health department, including Angie Salazar, now the acting director of ORR, John Fabbricatore , now a senior advisor at HHS, and Dawnisha Helland, the assistant principal deputy director of the unaccompanied alien children bureau at ORR.

Their roles at HHS give ICE a potential communication channel on issues involving unaccompanied children. "All these folks used to work together," one source said.

The Trump administration repeatedly argues that its custody and enforcement policies for unaccompanied children protect them from trafficking and being taken in by relatives who pose as safe and loving while preying on or exploiting them.

"ORR is not involved in the enforcement of immigration law or in the removal process. ORR is, however, involved in an inter-agency effort to locate children that arrived at the border alone during the Biden administration, and who were then release[d] to poorly vetted sponsors. In some cases, these sponsors exploited the unaccompanied children in their care, including through trafficking," the unnamed HHS spokesperson told the Guardian.

DHS echoed that sentiment, saying that its officials were dedicated to locating children "who came across the border unaccompanied [and] were placed with unvetted sponsors who were actually smugglers and sex traffickers".

But critics reiterated their argument that this perspective is exaggerated to the point of being disingenuous.

At the same time, the administration has implemented changes to reporting child trafficking concerns that could make it harder for survivors to win asylum and other immigration relief, the Associated Press reported .

Meanwhile, one expert told the Guardian that they did not know how officials at ORR could ever again reassure a prospective sponsor that it was safe to apply for a child's release, or tell a child that they were protected, with this administration's track record.

That expert fears that families across the globe whose children are fleeing gang conscription, violence and persecution will no longer look to the US for survival. They will be too afraid of the chances of a child being swiftly detained and deported even in the typical case where the child aims to join other family members living and working in the US.

"If you're that family and you have no option for your child to be safe except sending them to the United States, now that is off the table," the source said. "And so what happens to those kids?"

Will Craft and Andrew Witherspoon contributed reporting and graphics
